name: Carlos Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm at Hartley & Sons, a family agency on the high street in a market town, and I've been there six years now, mostly selling houses. Most days it's three or four viewings, a valuation if I'm lucky, then hours on the phone chasing solicitors about sales that are stuck. I like the viewings, honestly, walking a young couple round a semi and watching them start placing their sofa.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The chains. One buyer's mortgage wobbles and five families ring me in a day, all angry, and none of it is my fault. My pay is a basic plus commission, so a slow quarter shows up straight away in what I can put away. I've got about three months of bills saved and I'd like it to be more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Everyone at Hartley & Sons was nervous about the robots taking over, and it turned out to be a few apps. I'd probably joke about it at the pub with my mate Dev, who works at the bigger chain across the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life stays exactly as hard as it already is. AI wasn't my problem in the first place. My problem is a slow market, high mortgage rates and commission that can drop by a third in a bad spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the way I work now, and I mean that. I'd push to get more valuations in, because a valuation is where the next sale comes from. I'd also try to move another hundred a month into savings so a slow quarter stops scaring me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly, that I don't have to learn some new system. But it's not a calm feeling, because the money side is still bumpy. I'd still be checking my commission sheet every Friday with a knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a slow quarter scares you. What actually happens to your money in one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter I sold four houses in three months instead of the usual ten. My commission went from about nine hundred a month to under four hundred. Inés (my girlfriend) and I split the rent, so I just ate into the savings and stopped going out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there any routine tasks AI would take off you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the property write-ups, the bit where you describe the kitchen and the garden. Kirsty, our office manager, already tried one of those tools and the boss liked it. I'd let her do that and keep my hands on the phone.

say: The whole **AI scare** was overblown and the agency barely changed.
Selling houses still comes down to **people and phone calls**, like it always has.
think: My real worries are the **slow market** and high mortgage rates, not AI.
One bad spring can cut my **commission by a third**, and that stays true.
do: Carry on with the **same routine** of viewings, valuations and chasing solicitors.
Push for more **valuations** each month, since they lead to the next sales.
Move about **£100 more a month** into savings to soften slow quarters.
feel: Relieved there's **nothing new to learn**, but still tense about money.
Nervous every Friday when the **commission sheet** comes out.
S0.quote: AI wasn't my problem in the first place. My problem is a slow market, high mortgage rates and commission that can drop by a third in a bad spring.
fieldNote: He was **relieved** at the plateau, but his money worries were already there before AI.
His pay rides on **commission**, and he remembered last winter's numbers exactly.
He'd let a colleague use AI for write-ups rather than **touch it himself**.

steps.text: Keep doing three or four viewings a day at Hartley & Sons
Move an extra £100 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say people still want a person when they're spending their life savings. That's what I believe, mostly. I'd say it on the office group chat when the boss starts sending round articles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the people in the back office get hit first, and then it creeps up to me. Kirsty does the bookings, the letters and the chasing, and that's exactly the stuff on your card. If a computer books my viewings and writes my emails, the boss starts asking why he needs four negotiators instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and make sure my sales numbers are the best in the office, because that's my protection. I'd stop the takeaways and build the savings towards six months. If they made us use the AI system, I'd do the training, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor is tilting a bit. Not falling, just tilting. I don't sleep badly over it yet, but I'd be thinking about it on the drive between viewings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kirsty, first, because her whole job is the paperwork. Then Liam, the newest negotiator, because he's last in. I've been there six years, so I'd probably survive a cut, but I'm not the top seller either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the training but not go looking for it. Why hold back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every time I've tried a new system, it's slowed me down for months. The new property database last year took me ages and I lost a sale over a missed message. I'd rather be the guy who's good on the phone than the guy fiddling with screens.

say: Buyers still want **a real person** when they spend their life savings.
I'd push back on the **boss's articles** in the office group chat.
think: Back-office work like **bookings and letters** goes first, then it reaches me.
If software books viewings, the boss may keep **three negotiators** instead of four.
do: Aim to be the **top seller** in the office as protection against cuts.
Cut takeaways and build savings towards **six months** of bills.
Do the **AI training** only if the agency makes it compulsory.
feel: Uneasy, like the **floor is tilting** rather than falling.
S1.quote: If a computer books my viewings and writes my emails, the boss starts asking why he needs four negotiators instead of three.
fieldNote: He sees the **office manager's job** as the first to go, and his own next.
His defence is **sales numbers**, not new skills, which fits his dislike of new tech.
A bad experience with a **new database** last year still shapes how he sees tools.

steps.text: Push to be the top seller at Hartley & Sons this year
Build savings up towards six months of bills
Stop weekly takeaways and nights out for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it out loud at the pub: the job's done, lads, and nobody saw it coming. Then I'd laugh, because what else do you do. Online I wouldn't say anything, I never post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the agency shrinks to the boss and maybe one person doing viewings. The valuation, the listing, the negotiating by email, the chasing, all of that is thinking work, and your card says it goes in 2028. I'd have maybe three years of showing people round before a robot can do that too, and even then I'd be on lower pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking straight away for something with my hands, maybe with my uncle Jorge, who fits kitchens. I'd keep working at Hartley's as long as they'd have me and not spend a penny I don't need. Inés and I would put off looking for a place to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Two years is nothing. I've only just got good at this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Inés that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we stop talking about buying a flat for now. My girlfriend Inés is a dental hygienist, and that's hands-on, so she'd probably be fine longer than me. I'd hate being the one dragging us down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said kitchen fitting. You also said you avoid anything new. How does that fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. Fitting kitchens is new to me, but it's not a screen. I'd rather learn to use a drill from my uncle Jorge than learn to manage some AI system I don't trust.

say: The job's **done** and nobody saw it coming.
I'd joke about it at **the pub** but never post anything online.
think: The agency shrinks to **the boss** and one person doing viewings.
Viewings might last **three more years** before robots, on lower pay.
do: Ask **uncle Jorge** about learning to fit kitchens in the first year.
Keep working at Hartley's and **spend nothing extra**.
Put off **buying a flat** with Inés.
feel: Scared, because **two years** is no time to change course.
Guilty about being the one who **holds the couple back**.
S2.quote: My girlfriend Inés is a dental hygienist, and that's hands-on, so she'd probably be fine longer than me. I'd hate being the one dragging us down.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose most** of his job, with viewings as a short reprieve.
He'd pick **hands-on work** with family over learning AI, despite fearing new things.
Shame about being **the weaker earner** came through more than fear of money itself.

steps.text: Learn kitchen fitting with uncle Jorge on weekends
Cut all spending except rent, bills and food
Put plans to buy a flat with Inés on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and we'd better be ready, which is what everyone would be saying by then. I'd say it at work in the Monday meeting when the boss asked for ideas. I wouldn't have many ideas, mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but I don't think it changes where I end up. The thinking part of my job goes in 2031 and the showing round goes around 2034. I'd be thirty-two, with no degree and a skill nobody wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hartley's for maybe two more years and save hard, because the commission is still there for now. Then I'd start an evening course, maybe electrics, so I'm qualified before 2031. I'd keep the savings at six months minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a slower kind of worried. I can see a path, I just don't like any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrics, and why wait two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin did his electrics at night school and he's never short of work. I'd wait because I want the commission while it lasts, and because maybe it doesn't happen. That's me, I always wait a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. I'd swap it for something cheaper and older, which hurts because I need it for viewings. And holidays, we'd just stay home.

say: It's **coming** and the office had better be ready.
I wouldn't have many ideas for the boss's **Monday meeting**.
think: Five years doesn't change **where I end up**, only when.
By 2031 I'd be thirty-two with **no degree** and a fading skill.
do: Stay at Hartley's **two more years** to bank commission while it lasts.
Start an **evening electrics course** so I'm qualified before 2031.
Keep savings at **six months** minimum and swap to a cheaper car.
feel: Worried, but **slower and steadier** than the two-year picture.
S3.quote: The thinking part of my job goes in 2031 and the showing round goes around 2034. I'd be thirty-two, with no degree and a skill nobody wants.
fieldNote: He'd use the extra time to **bank commission**, not to move early.
He named his own habit of **waiting a bit** without being asked.
Choosing **electrics** came from his cousin's example, not from research.

steps.text: Keep selling at Hartley's for two more years while commission lasts
Enrol in an evening electrics course by 2028
Swap the car for an older, cheaper one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so stop panicking. I'd say that to Kirsty and Liam especially, because they'd be the ones worrying. I'd probably believe it too, for the first few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years is enough that I'd waste five of them. I know myself. But it does mean I could sell houses into my thirties and maybe buy a place with Inés before it all shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and try to buy a small flat with Inés in the next three or four years, while we both have steady pay. Somewhere around 2031 I'd start a trade course for real. I'd keep a bit aside every month as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, honestly. It's still a cliff at the end, but I can see it from far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste five of the years. What would make you not waste them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone I know got hit first. If Dev lost his job at the chain across the road, I'd move that week. Without that I'd just keep telling myself there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would buying a flat be a risk, if your income might go later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But rent's dead money, and Inés is the steady one. If we buy small and fix the rate for five years, I think we could carry it even if I'm retraining.

say: We've got **ten years** before anything big happens, so stop panicking.
I'd say it to **Kirsty and Liam** first, since they'd be the ones worrying.
think: Ten years is long enough that I'd **waste five** of them.
It could let me **buy a flat** with Inés before things shift.
do: Keep selling and try to **buy a small flat** within four years.
Start a **trade course** around 2031 if nothing pushes me sooner.
Fix the **mortgage rate** for five years to keep costs steady.
feel: Calmer, because the **cliff** is far away.
Aware I'd need a **shock nearby** to actually move.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough that I'd waste five of them. I know myself.
fieldNote: He was **honest about delay**: only a friend losing his job would push him.
The long timeline turns his thoughts to **buying a home**, not his career.
He still expects to **lose the job** in the end, so the worry stays.

steps.text: Keep selling homes at Hartley's for now
Buy a small flat with Inés on a five-year fixed rate

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because I'd have no time and no plan B. What would help is a proper paid route into a trade, like an apprenticeship that pays enough for rent, not just a website telling me to reskill. And maybe the agency being straight with us early instead of after it's decided.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what buyers would want. My older buyers already hate the online portals, and I think some would pay extra for a person. Whether that's enough people to keep an office open, I don't know.

headlineQuote: I'd rather learn to use a drill from my uncle Jorge than learn to manage some AI system I don't trust.
portrait: A **27-year-old** sales negotiator at a family agency on a market-town high street, six years in.
Paid **basic plus commission**, with about three months saved and money already tight in slow seasons.
Avoids **new technology** and trusts phone skills and relationships over software.
Gets more **alarmed** as timelines shorten and would turn to hands-on trades through family.
Admits he tends to **wait**, and would likely only move if someone close got hit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to build a plan B.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** route into a trade that covers rent.
His agency being **honest early** about plans to cut staff.
